meta: Dramas like Dear My Friends: six shows that treat old age, and ordinary life, as a real subject.
standfirst: A group of women in their seventies, a writer in her late thirties recording them, and sixteen hours that refuse to make anybody wise or cute. Noh Hee Kyung's argument is that the last third of a life is still a life with wants in it. These six sit near that, and we say which ones share the argument and which only share the warmth.

picks.why: The same writer, the same conviction, twenty episodes on Jeju. Noh Hee Kyung again handing whole chapters to middle-aged and older characters and writing their wants at full size, with an ensemble that includes the best work Lee Byung Hun has done on television. Same structure of separate lives touching at the edges. Difference: it is an anthology, so each story gets a clean shape, where Dear My Friends lets everything overlap and stay unresolved.

One old person, one want, twelve episodes. A seventy year old retired postman decides to learn ballet and the show treats the decision with total seriousness, never once using him as a lesson for a younger character. Same refusal of sentimentality about aging. Difference: it is a two-hander rather than an ensemble, and the sadness is one specific medical fact rather than the general weather.

Kim Hye Ja again, and the same question from the other end. A young woman who can bend time and ages decades in an instant, so she has to live as the person Dear My Friends is about. Both are ultimately about how it feels to be looked past. Difference: it is built on a fantasy device and a twist, and the ending recasts everything you have watched, which this one would never do.

Same writer, working life instead of late life. A patrol division staffed by people who took the job because nothing else was available, written with Noh Hee Kyung's usual attention to what people say when nothing is happening. Same faith that ordinary competence is dramatic. Difference: the register is procedural and the jeopardy is physical, so it is far less interior.

Sixty years of one family, told at the same patient speed. Four seasons, one Jeju household, and a script that treats ordinary lives as worth sixteen hours because they are. Same argument about parents having been people first. Difference: it is a life told forward from youth, so it gives you the reward of watching somebody grow up, which Dear My Friends deliberately denies you.

The same writer's other subject. A novelist, a psychiatrist and a shared house, with mental illness written as something to live with rather than a plot device, and the dialogue rhythms are unmistakably hers. Difference: it is a romance with young leads at the centre, so the generational subject is background rather than the point.

against.title: Reply 1988
against.why: Handed over whenever anybody asks for warmth about family, and the parents in it are genuinely well written. It is still a nostalgia show narrated by the children: the older characters exist in relation to them. Dear My Friends puts the older characters at the centre and lets the young narrator be the one who does not understand.

against.title: Hospital Playlist
against.why: The comfort recommendation by reflex. It is a hangout show about competent people in their forties enjoying each other, with no interest in decline, dependence or money, which is most of what Dear My Friends is about.

against.title: Curtain Call
against.why: Pitched as the other drama about a dying grandmother, and it turns the premise into a con-artist plot with a romance attached. The grandmother becomes the reason for the scheme rather than a person with her own last chapter.
